scope: Independent second review of all modern new edges, translations, stories and borrowing descriptions. Legacy claims retain the baseline review; Coldplay interpolation checked against both original sources again.
hashEncoding: SHA-256 of UTF-8 json.dumps(link, ensure_ascii=False, sort_keys=True, separators=(comma,colon)); covers the whole link.

entries.claim: Massive Attack sampled Billy Cobham's 'Stratus' in 'Safe from Harm'.
entries.evidence: Cobham explicitly discusses permission for the sample in the interview; Grossmann identifies backing phrases from Stratus (Spectrum, 1973), p. 97. PDF downloaded and text read independently.

entries.claim: James Brown's funk was an influence on Kraftwerk.
entries.evidence: Bartos names Brown and funk in the interview; Croatian Encyclopedia separately identifies Brown/funk as an influence.

entries.claim: Radiohead drew on Charles Mingus's jazz for 'Pyramid Song'.
entries.evidence: Prog identifies Mingus as a source for Pyramid Song; Colin Greenwood confirms the connection in the Irish Times interview.

entries.claim: Nina Simone's version of 'Wild Is the Wind' inspired David Bowie to record it for Station to Station.
entries.evidence: NPO describes Bowie following Simone; Verve/UMe notes that Simone inspired the Station to Station recording. This is a cover, not a sample.

entries.claim: Talking Heads drew on Fela Kuti's Afrobeat when making Remain in Light.
entries.evidence: Library of Congress essay describes the Fela-inspired jams; Pitchfork independently identifies Afrodisiac as the model.

entries.claim: Peter Gabriel made 'Sledgehammer' as a tribute to the soul music of Otis Redding.
entries.evidence: Gabriel calls Sledgehammer a homage to formative soul music and names Redding; the 1987 Sound On Sound interview supplies independent first-person testimony.

entries.claim: The Clash recorded a cover of Junior Murvin’s reggae song “Police and Thieves”.
entries.evidence: Official album notes and Pitchfork independently identify the Murvin cover on the debut album.

entries.claim: The Prodigy's 'Smack My Bitch Up' samples 'Give the Drummer Some' by Ultramagnetic MCs.
entries.evidence: MusicTech identifies Kool Keith’s isolated vocal hook; Morey independently identifies Give the Drummer Some as the sampled recording. Both fetched documents read locally.

entries.claim: Paul Simon recorded 'Mother and Child Reunion' in Jamaica with musicians who had backed Jimmy Cliff.
entries.evidence: Jamaica Observer identifies Jimmy Cliff’s backing musicians; NPO independently describes that Jamaican recording session.

entries.claim: James Brown carried gospel vocal intensity into his rhythm-and-blues and funk.
entries.evidence: Rock Hall describes gospel vocal fervor; Inayatullah independently discusses Brown carrying gospel singing into funk.

entries.claim: Fela Kuti developed Afrobeat by combining West African highlife, jazz and American soul and funk.
entries.evidence: Rock Hall and Trinity Laban independently describe the highlife/jazz/American soul-funk fusion.

entries.claim: James Brown’s funk helped shape Fela Kuti’s music.
entries.evidence: Rock Hall names Brown; Inayatullah independently traces the Brown connection.

entries.claim: The church music Charles Mingus heard as a child was one of his earliest musical influences.
entries.evidence: Mingus estate and Blue Note both identify childhood church music as an early influence.

entries.claim: Charles Mingus brought gospel into his jazz compositions.
entries.evidence: Blue Note identifies gospel as a compositional ingredient; Doug Hall at WICN independently discusses Better Git It in Your Soul and childhood gospel.

entries.claim: Billy Cobham played drums with Miles Davis before his work in the Mahavishnu Orchestra.
entries.evidence: Blue Note places Davis before Mahavishnu; Cobham independently discusses his Davis period and the fusion band. Do not repeat Blue Note’s erroneous Bitches Brew credit.

entries.claim: Billy Cobham’s work with the Mahavishnu Orchestra placed him in the early jazz-fusion movement.
entries.evidence: Blue Note and the independently conducted Cobham interview both identify Mahavishnu as early jazz fusion.

entries.claim: Otis Redding’s musical upbringing was rooted in singing in church.
entries.evidence: Georgia Encyclopedia and American National Biography both establish church singing in his upbringing.

entries.claim: Edwin Birdsong developed jazz-funk records in collaboration with Roy Ayers.
entries.evidence: Resident Advisor describes Birdsong’s Roy Ayers collaboration; Wax Poetics independently describes their jazz-funk records.

entries.claim: Daft Punk built “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger” around a sample of Edwin Birdsong’s “Cola Bottle Baby”.
entries.evidence: Resident Advisor and Radio Milwaukee both identify the 1979 Cola Bottle Baby recording as the sampled basis. Instrumental groove describes the borrowed accompaniment, not a vocal sample.

entries.claim: Ultramagnetic MCs grew out of Bronx DJ culture, with Ced Gee moving from DJing into rap and sample-based production.
entries.evidence: SPIN’s independent interview describes Bronx DJ beginnings and funk-sample production; Ced Gee’s official biography supplies his DJ-to-rapper progression.

entries.claim: Dr. Dre built the G-funk sound of The Chronic around Parliament-Funkadelic’s grooves.
entries.evidence: Rashad Grove’s Library of Congress essay and Sheldon Pearce’s Pitchfork review independently describe Parliament-Funkadelic grooves reshaped through samples and live instrumentation.

entries.claim: Arctic Monkeys drew on Dr. Dre’s hip-hop rhythms when making AM.
entries.evidence: Radio X quotes Turner’s NME description of a Dre beat; Enmore quotes a separate Uncut interview about Dre-like grooves.

entries.claim: King Tubby developed dub by remixing Jamaican rhythm tracks, dropping parts in and out and adding echo.
entries.evidence: Reggaeville describes dropping instrumental parts and adding echoes; Williams examines the faders, four-track remixing and tape-delay system.

entries.claim: Lee “Scratch” Perry helped develop dub through experiments with reggae rhythm tracks and studio effects.
entries.evidence: Resident Advisor describes Perry’s experimental dub production; Danny Kelly’s archived NME interview records Perry describing rhythm-track and effects experiments.

entries.claim: King Tubby mixed Lee “Scratch” Perry’s Blackboard Jungle Dub.
entries.evidence: David Katz and Sean Williams both identify Tubby’s mixing contribution. Katz notes disputed division of labor; claim does not assign exclusive authorship or a disputed release year.

entries.claim: Lee “Scratch” Perry produced the Clash’s “Complete Control”.
entries.evidence: Official single notes credit Perry; Danny Kelly’s NME interview independently identifies the co-production. Producer kind does not imply sole production.

entries.claim: Lee “Scratch” Perry produced Junior Murvin’s breakthrough “Police and Thieves”.
entries.evidence: Pitchfork identifies Perry’s production of the breakthrough; Murvin independently recalls working with and learning from Perry.

entries.claim: Junior Murvin’s “Police and Thieves” emerged from Jamaica’s reggae recording scene.
entries.evidence: Pitchfork situates the record in Jamaican reggae; Murvin’s independent interview describes the reggae recording context.

entries.claim: Lee “Scratch” Perry helped the Wailers develop their sound by pairing them with bassist Aston Barrett and drummer Carlton Barrett.
entries.evidence: Marley estate and Cambridge Companion profile both describe Perry adding the Barrett rhythm section and shaping the group’s sound.

entries.claim: The Wailers’ work with Lee “Scratch” Perry helped define roots reggae.
entries.evidence: Marley estate calls the Perry sessions a paradigm for roots reggae; Cambridge independently identifies their formative reggae sound.

entries.claim: The Police drew on Bob Marley’s reggae when developing their bass-led grooves.
entries.evidence: Spicer documents Marley’s effect on Police bass patterns through Sting and Summers testimony; Summers’ separate FretBuzz interview places reggae/Marley in their environment and explains the bass approach. This does not classify the Police as a reggae band.

entries.claim: Bob Marley was an influence on Aquarium’s Boris Grebenshchikov.
entries.evidence: Archived official Blue Album notes place Marley listening in Aquarium’s reggae period; Bakanov’s independent Sobesednik profile names Marley among Grebenshchikov’s strongest influences.

entries.claim: Jimmy Cliff began singing in church before his recording career.
entries.evidence: Kreps in Rolling Stone and NPR’s independent report (including Cliff’s own archival testimony) both identify childhood gospel church singing.
